name: Pantheism and the non-distinctness of creature from Creator
plain_explanation: John the Scot holds that the created world is not something separate from God but subsists within God; 'the creature is not a being distinct from God,' and God manifests Himself in the creature 'in an ineffable manner.' Creation is described as an eternal process, and the substance of all finite things is said to be God Himself.
precise_definition: The doctrine that finite creatures do not possess independent substantial existence apart from God, but exist as manifestations or emanations of the divine substance -- in Russell's words, a pantheism that 'refuses substantial reality to creatures.'
why_it_mattered: This view is explicitly heretical by orthodox Christian standards (which require a real distinction between Creator and creature), and it is the central charge against John the Scot's orthodoxy, alongside his unusual account of the Trinity.
historical_origin: Rooted in Neoplatonic emanationism, transmitted to John the Scot chiefly through his translation of the pseudo-Dionysius rather than through direct knowledge of Plotinus or Proclus, whom Russell says he probably never read.
examples: "The Holy Trinity loves Itself in us and in Itself; It sees and moves Itself."
God's interpretation of creation 'out of nothing' as meaning creation out of God Himself, understood as transcending all knowledge
objections: Russell notes that his Trinity, closely resembling that of Plotinus, fails to preserve the equality of the Three Persons, though John tries to safeguard himself on this point
competing_positions: Orthodox Christian doctrine, which requires creatures to be really distinct from their Creator
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly conflicts with Church doctrine on creation and the Trinity, leading to repeated condemnation.
